node.label: Gabrielle M. Spiegel
node.date_label: Social Logic of the Text (1990) · Romancing the Past (1993) · The Past as Text (1997) · Practicing History, editor (2005)
node.description: Gabrielle M. Spiegel argues that historical texts must be read both as literary forms and as interventions in particular social settings: their social logic. She developed this approach in “History, Historicism, and the Social Logic of the Text in the Middle Ages” (1990) and applied it in Romancing the Past (1993), explaining how a small group of threatened Franco-Flemish patrons used vernacular prose histories to defend aristocratic legitimacy. Robert M. Stein describes her position as a “middle ground” in which historians read documents deconstructively while still treating language as conveying information about past lives. Raymond Cormier’s 1995 review praises the book’s argument while faulting its treatment of literary commonplaces and epic distinctions, and suggesting that comparable ideological uses of antiquity appeared earlier under Henry II. The Past as Text (1997) collected her essays; Practicing History (2005), which she edited and introduced, examined historical writing after the linguistic turn. Her later work distinguishes memory from historical time and asks how historians can acknowledge mediation while attending to an absent past.
node.representative_figures_and_works: The Chronicle Tradition of Saint-Denis: A Survey (1978); “History, Historicism, and the Social Logic of the Text in the Middle Ages” (1990); Romancing the Past (1993; paperback 1995); The Past as Text (1997); “Memory and History: Liturgical Time and Historical Time” (2002); Practicing History (2005), editor and introduction; “The Task of the Historian” (2009).
node.scope_note: Romancing the Past acknowledgments, introduction and introduction notes read; remaining chapters not surveyed. The 1990 essay is known here through Stein’s named account, bibliographic records and the 1993 formulation, not a fresh complete reading. The Past as Text and Practicing History are not read in full. Selected main-text passages and notes of the 2009 address, the complete 2018 White essay and Cormier’s complete review were read. The 2002 memory article is supported only by its publisher abstract. The Stone and Eley exchange bodies remain unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In "The Task of the Historian" (2009) Spiegel takes Derridean deconstruction as the key expression of the linguistic turn and reads it as a philosophy shaped by the Holocaust, while adopting its lesson of listening for silence.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Spiegel's AHA presidential address (2009), historians.org: 'I will take Derridean deconstruction as the key expression of the impulses at work in generating the linguistic turn'; 'Derrida alchemized into philosophy a psychology deeply marked by the Holocaust'; n. 14 'Derrida does not, however, specify the "event" he calls a rupture'; and the adopted lesson of 'listening to silence'. Reversed and retyped from a journalist's profile on Fable's reading (F07-029).
proposed_edges.map_label: Deconstruction as the linguistic turn, read historically

proposed_edges.relationship: In The Task of the Historian (2009), Spiegel uses de Certeau’s separation of present and past to frame historical writing as an engagement with absence.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Address, paragraphs beginning One of the most significant characteristics through The historian’s task, and note 7: The Writing of History, English translation (1988), p. 5. De Certeau’s book unread here. Quoted phrase: “engagement with absence”.
proposed_edges.map_label: De Certeau on the absent past

proposed_edges.relationship: In Romancing the Past (1993), Spiegel uses Raymond Williams’s account of the continuing production of cultural orders to frame aristocratic historical writing.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Introduction p. 5 and p. 325 n. 2: Culture (1981), p. 201, explicitly cited through Alan Sinfield’s typescript. A mediated resource; neither original read here. Quoted phrase: “actively made”.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Romancing the Past (1993), Spiegel uses Le Goff’s account of social change to connect material conditions with aristocratic imaginative worlds.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Introduction p. 5; p. 325 n. 3 names the essay on Jacques de Vitry in The Medieval Imagination, English translation (1988), p. 181. The quoted essay is unread here. Quoted phrase: “material and imaginary realities”.
proposed_edges.map_label: Le Goff on social and imaginary change

proposed_edges.relationship: In Hayden White’s Return to the Past as a Source of Human Practice (2018), Spiegel interprets White’s practical past as the culmination of his concern with ethical choice and freedom from inherited historical necessity.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Complete journal PDF, pp. 127–135, especially pp. 129–130 and 133–134. An affirmative reception argument, not a critique or proof of personal collaboration. White’s underlying works remain unread in this dossier. Quoted phrase: “logical culmination”.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Romancing the Past (1993), Spiegel joins formal analysis to the social setting of historical texts.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Introduction pp. 9–10, “social logic”; existing language roster retained. New timeline edge; no existing person edge.

proposed_edges.relationship: Romancing the Past (1993) explains vernacular prose as an ideological resource of threatened Franco-Flemish patrons.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Introduction pp. 2–4 and 9–10; selected patrons, not all nobles. Whole book unread. Quoted phrase: “small group of patrons”.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Memory and History: Liturgical Time and Historical Time (2002), Spiegel contests the collapse of history into memory by distinguishing their temporal structures.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher abstract, final paragraph, explicitly contests conflation. Abstract only; no claim to reading the article body or to all forms of memory. Quoted phrase: “collapse history into memory”.

proposed_edges.relationship: In The Task of the Historian (2009), Spiegel presents practice as a way to connect discursive formation with individual initiative.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Address, paragraphs beginning As William Sewell and Culture, thereby, notes 35–37; also note 49. Specific proposal; no assertion of a consensus replacing poststructuralism. Practicing History (2005) unread. Quoted phrase: “discursive constitution and individual initiative”.

proposed_edges.relationship: In ‘The Task of the Historian’ (2009), Spiegel argued that historians moving beyond the linguistic turn should retain poststructuralism’s insights into rupture, displacement and the mediation of historical knowledge.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the AHA’s primary text, particularly the discussion following notes 38–41. Spiegel accepts that historical concerns are changing but questions discarding poststructuralist insights; the following paragraphs explain their continuing relevance. Robert A. Schneider’s February 2009 AHR introduction independently identifies this as an argument for preserving core features of poststructuralism. This records a substantive intervention in the debate, not evidence that a particular historian adopted it. The address was delivered in January and published in February 2009; 2008 identifies Spiegel’s presidential term, not the work’s publication year.
proposed_edges.map_label: What to retain after the linguistic turn

proposed_edges.relationship: In ‘The Task of the Historian’ (2009), Spiegel proposed that transnational and diaspora history examine losses of cultural identity accompanying migration, qualifying accounts that celebrate mobility and hybridity.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the primary discussion of transnational history and diaspora studies, from the paragraph preceding note 42 through the discussion following note 46. Spiegel explicitly proposes investigating losses associated with migration, exile and diasporic movement, and identifies celebratory accounts of transnationalism as the position to qualify. The existing global endpoint is the umbrella for this transnational intervention. The claim concerns her methodological proposal, not demonstrated adoption by the field. Schneider’s February 2009 AHR introduction also connects her concluding argument to transnational experiences of migration and displacement. This target pair is absent from the input; the edge records a specific intervention in transnational historiography rather than another general memory or language contribution.
